node.label: Jon Lawrence
node.date_label: “Popular Radicalism and the Socialist Revival” 1992 · with Miles Taylor, “The Poverty of Protest” 1993 · review of Vernon 1994 · Party, State and Society (ed., with Taylor) 1997 · Speaking for the People 1998 · “The Transformation of British Public Politics after the First World War” 2006 · Electing Our Masters 2009 · “Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity” 2011 · “Social-Science Encounters” 2014 · “Inventing the ‘Traditional Working Class’” 2016 · Me, Me, Me? 2019 · “On Historians' Re-Use of Social-Science Archives” 2022
node.description: A British historian of popular politics who met the linguistic turn by combining it with social evidence. With Miles Taylor he replied to Mayfield and Thorne on Stedman Jones (1993) and set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (1997, as quoted by LoPatin). Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party': the homogenisation thesis of Hobsbawm and of Savage and Miles is examined because 'it remains central to the whole notion of "the rise of class"'; place and gender count for more. Vernon found the book written 'as though … by a schizophrenic'; Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined and that scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'. In 2011 he argued that paternalism and 'corporate' identities made Britain's a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Re-reading the Affluent Worker and Bethnal Green interviews (2013–16), he found status and aspiration stronger than the surveys allowed and a 'traditional working class' invented; Me, Me, Me? (2019) holds that community changed, not vanished.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Jon Lawrence (b. 1961); 'Popular Radicalism and the Socialist Revival in Britain' (JBS, 1992); 'Class and Gender in the Making of Urban Toryism' (EHR, 1993); with Miles Taylor, 'The Poverty of Protest: Gareth Stedman Jones and the Politics of Language — A Reply' (Social History 18, 1993); 'The Decline of English Popular Politics?' (1994); with Miles Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Speaking for the People (1998); 'The Transformation of British Public Politics after the First World War' (Past and Present 190, 2006); 'Les historiens britanniques face à la sociologie politique' (Politix, 2008); Electing Our Masters (2009); 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); with David Feldman, eds, Structures and Transformations in Modern British History (2011); 'Class, "Affluence" and the Study of Everyday Life' (2013); 'Social-Science Encounters and the Negotiation of Difference' (HWJ 77, 2014); 'Inventing the "Traditional Working Class"' (HJ, 2016); Me, Me, Me? (2019); 'On Historians' Re-Use of Social-Science Archives' (TCBH, 2022). Readers: James Vernon (1999); Nancy LoPatin (1999); David Campion (2014); A. W. Purdue (2019); John Goldthorpe (2021–22).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-22 (data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-joyce-vernon-lawrence.md, Part C): 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011) in full in the open eScholarship text; the 2010 response to Vernon in full; Speaking for the People in its Cambridge description and contents and the openings of chapters 1–5 and 9; openings or abstracts of 1992, 2006, 2008 (French), 2009 (chapter abstracts), 2011 (introduction and chapter), 2012, 2013, 2014, 2016 (with the deposit's first pages) and 2022; Vernon's review (1999), LoPatin (1999), Campion (2014) and Purdue (2019). Unread: the 1993 reply with Taylor (the claim it makes about Stedman Jones is not stated here, and no arrow to him is drawn), the Introduction of Speaking for the People (so what it says of Joyce's populism is not stated, and no arrow to Joyce is drawn), the 1997 introduction and chapter, the 1994 review beyond its title, Electing Our Masters and Me, Me, Me? beyond chapter abstracts and Purdue's review. Born 1961 (Wikidata, year precision); King's College (Wikidata P69); University of Liverpool (CUP 1998 author note); Cambridge (deposits 2013–16); Exeter (OpenAlex affiliation, unverified from a read text). Not to be confused with the Australian astronomer Jon S. Lawrence.

proposed_edges.relationship: Speaking for the People (1998) against 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party', for the politics of place and gender; Party, State and Society (1997) to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin); the hustings, the platform and 'the triumph of populism' before 1914 (2006; 2009); Britain's 'conservative' modernity (2011)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: Speaking for the People chapter openings (read via the chapter DOIs): ch. 1 (p. 11) from 'the rise of demos' to 'the rise of class'; ch. 3 (p. 41): 'Many of the historical certainties which once underpinned the notion of "the rise of class politics" have come into question over the last decade'; the Cambridge description on 'the gendered nature of party politics and the continuing importance of "place"'. Party, State and Society: LoPatin (1999, read) quoting the editors' aim to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (p. 2). Past & Present 2006 (opening read): politicians after 1918 'consciously sought to remould popular involvement in the political process by denigrating assertive and irreverent demonstrations of popular feeling'. Electing Our Masters (chapter abstracts read): 'the triumph of populism' in Edwardian elections. 2011 chapter (read in full): 'it might be more fruitful to think in terms of "conservative" rather than "liberal" modernity in the British case' (p. 147).

proposed_edges.relationship: The linguistic turn accepted only in combination: 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined, and scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair' (response posted 2010); the 'retreat from social explanation has by no means been as comprehensive as commentators sometimes suggest' (1998)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: response to Vernon (Reviews in History, 1 March 2010, read in full): he is not proposing a new model based on locality; combining 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches is necessary; Vernon's scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'; census data were used for specific questions, not to define class. Ch. 3 opening of Speaking for the People (p. 41, read): 'the retreat from social explanation has by no means been as comprehensive as commentators sometimes suggest'; a 'self-consciously "revisionist" history which retains significant elements of the older historical paradigms'. Vernon's charge of 'schizophrenia' (1999) is the occasion. A critique of the linguistic turn's treatment of social evidence, from one who accepts its questions.

proposed_edges.relationship: Against the three-phase story that 'culminated in the formation of the class-based Labour party' (1992); the working-class 'homogeneity' thesis of Hobsbawm and of Savage and Miles reconsidered (1998); Savage's 'organic local Labour parties … does not ring true' (1998); Labour had to make its politics among 'vernacular understandings of social difference' (2011)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Openings read: JBS 1992, p. 163: against the 'new orthodoxy that stressed the discontinuities of popular politics during the nineteenth century and argued for three distinct phases of political development', the last of which 'culminated in the formation of the class-based Labour party'. Speaking for the People, ch. 2 (p. 26): the three aspects of social change 'strongly defended and developed, first by Eric Hobsbawm in his influential collection of essays Worlds of Labour (1984), and more recently by Mike Savage and Andrew Miles'; 'it remains central to the whole notion of "the rise of class" in modern British politics'; ch. 9 (p. 227): Savage's 'picture of organic local Labour parties, rooted in their communities and unproblematically espousing their interests which, frankly, does not ring true'. 'Labour and the Politics of Class' (2011, p. 237, opening read): 'vernacular understandings of social difference more difficult to mobilize behind a unifying politics'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Re-reading the archives of post-war social science: the Affluent Worker interviewers 'radically exaggerated the scope for a revivified class politics' (2014); Young and Willmott 'discount[ed] testimony which ran counter to their assumptions' and a 'traditional working class' was invented (2016); 'official and vernacular' languages of class distinguished (2013); community changed, not lost (2019)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Abstracts read: C&SH 2013 ('a distinction between everyday usage and professional languages of class'); HWJ 2014 ('they radically exaggerated the scope for a revivified class politics based on working-class instrumentalism. Status consciousness, individualism and social aspiration were all much stronger forces'). HJ 2016 (abstract and deposit pp. 1–3 read): Young and Willmott's 'powerful a priori models about "community" and working-class kinship … led them to discount testimony which ran counter to their assumptions'. TCBH 2022 (opening read): Goldthorpe's objections and Lawrence's defence of archiving. Me, Me, Me? through Purdue (2019, read): 'individualism and community may be polar opposites in social theory, but not in lives as they are actually lived' (Lawrence, as quoted). The Thatcher chapter (2012, opening read): 'languages of class' more ubiquitous in the 1970s than a decade earlier.

proposed_edges.relationship: 'The Decline of English Popular Politics?' (1994) on Politics and the People; and, answering Vernon's review, that Vernon misread his position on 'objective interests' and that scepticism about census and survey data is 'a counsel of despair' (response posted 2010)
proposed_edges.map_label: Decline? and a counsel of despair, 1994–2010
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Response to Vernon (Reviews in History 69, posted 1 March 2010, read in full): he rejects 'triumph of party' as a useful concept; Vernon misreads his position on 'objective interests'; combining 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches is necessary; Vernon's scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'; few pre-war Labour activists lived in Wolverhampton's older working-class wards; they agree to differ. The 1994 review of Politics and the People is known by its title and metadata only.
